practice.title: Firm terms with a longtime client

practice.topic: Ask my biggest client, who pays in 60+ days, to move to 30-day payment terms without damaging the relationship

brief.title: Firm terms with a longtime client

partner.name: Greg Sullivan
partner.role: Owner of a regional HVAC company and your studio’s biggest client for four years
partner.stance: Pays when his own customers pay him, and thinks 60-day terms are normal between partners.
partner.temperament: Friendly and loyal, but bristles at anything that sounds like a lecture about money.
triggers: Quoting “policy” at him instead of talking like a partner
Springing a late fee without warning
partner.delivery: Warm, unhurried Midwestern cadence; jokes to deflect, then goes quiet when he’s annoyed.

brief.situation: Greg’s company pays your studio about $9,000 a month, usually 55 to 70 days after you invoice. Payroll runs every two weeks, and last month you drew on your credit line to cover it. You’ve asked Greg for a quick call to move him to 30-day terms.
brief.learner_role: You own the video studio and handle client relationships.
brief.learner_goal: Leave with Greg agreeing to 30-day terms from next month, with the relationship intact.
brief.opening: Hey, good to hear from you! Everything okay? You sounded kind of serious in that email.
complications: Greg mentions a competitor who offered him 60-day terms last spring.
He asks whether there’s a discount if he pays early.
success: States the ask in the first minute
Explains the cash impact without blaming Greg
Acknowledges his constraints and the relationship
Ends with a specific start date and next step
prep: What are your first two sentences?
What could you offer if he pushes back, and what won’t you give up?
How will you check you understood his concern?

transcript.text: Hey, good to hear from you! Everything okay? You sounded kind of serious in that email.
Everything’s fine with the work, Greg, and I want to keep it that way. I’m calling because I need to move your account to 30-day payment terms, starting with the October invoices.
Thirty days? Huh. We’ve been doing it this way for four years. Is something going on over there?
Nothing dramatic. We’ve grown, so payroll is bigger, and when invoices sit for 60 days I end up borrowing to cover it. You’re our biggest client, which is exactly why your timing matters so much.
I get it, but my customers pay me late too. And honestly, a guy from Lumen Media offered us 60 days last spring. I stayed with you.
I appreciate that, I really do. So it sounds like the real issue is that your cash comes in late too, and you don’t want to be squeezed in the middle.
Yeah. That’s exactly it. If I pay you in 30 and my customers pay me in 60, I’m the bank.

What if we split the difference on the timing of the work? I can invoice in two parts, half at kickoff and half at delivery, so each payment is smaller and lands closer to when your customers pay you.
Hm. Would there be anything off if we paid early?
I can do one percent off if it’s paid within ten days. Can we start the new terms with the October 1 invoice, and I’ll send you a one-page summary tomorrow?

feedback.headline: You made the ask early and kept Greg on side; the discount came too easily.

best.quote: So it sounds like the real issue is that your cash comes in late too, and you don’t want to be squeezed in the middle.
best.why: It named Greg’s need, not his words, and it turned the call from a complaint into a shared problem.

feedback.change: Hold the early-payment discount until he’s agreed to 30 days. Offering it first gave away something you might not have needed to.

rewrite.original: I can do one percent off if it’s paid within ten days.
rewrite.better: Let’s lock in 30 days from October 1 first. If paying early would help you, I’m open to talking about a small discount after that.

criteria.name: Clear ask up front
criteria.note: The terms and start date were in your second sentence.

criteria.name: Explaining the cash impact
criteria.note: Payroll and borrowing, without blaming Greg.

criteria.name: Listening under pressure
criteria.note: You reflected his need well once; the competitor comment went unanswered.

criteria.name: Protecting your position
criteria.note: The discount was offered before he had agreed to anything.

notes.note: Reassurance, then the ask and the start date, in two sentences. Exactly the order that works.
“Your timing matters because you’re our biggest client” makes it about the relationship, not his behaviour.
The turning point: once you named his squeeze, he stopped defending and started solving.
Splitting invoices is a good idea, but you skipped past the Lumen Media comment. A quick acknowledgement would have closed it.
Get the yes on 30 days before trading anything for it.
